answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This line is Fitzgerald's own — entry 330 of his private notebooks, filed under the heading “E: Epigrams, Wisecracks, and Jokes.” The version that circulates online has been lightly smoothed: Fitzgerald actually wrote “you write because you've got something to say,” with a semicolon, not a comma.

source.excerpt: You don't write because you want to say something; you write because you've got something to say.
trail: Entry 330 of Fitzgerald's manuscript notebooks, under “E: Epigrams, Wisecracks, and Jokes,” reads “You don't write because you want to say something; you write because you've got something to say” — see the full transcription of Notebook E ↗.
Wikiquote's Fitzgerald page ↗ cites this same line to Notebook E as it appeared in The Crack-Up (1945), edited by Edmund Wilson.
The complete, numbered edition of the notebooks was later published as The Notebooks of F. Scott Fitzgerald ↗ (1978), edited by Matthew J. Bruccoli.
LibQuotes ↗ independently traces the quote to the same “Note-Books” section of the 1945 Wilson edition.
source.excerptNote: Fitzgerald's own wording, as transcribed from Notebook E, entry 330. The widely shared internet version reads “…you write because you have something to say,” swapping in “have” for “'ve got” and a comma for the semicolon.

author.name: F. Scott Fitzgerald
author.heading: About F. Scott Fitzgerald
author.bio: Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was a chronicler of the Jazz Age, best known for The Great Gatsby (1925) and Tender Is the Night (1934). Throughout his career he kept private notebooks — running lists of overheard lines, epigrams, and story ideas — which he mined for his fiction and which were published only after his death.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This one really is Fitzgerald's, but the popular wording isn't quite what he wrote.

items.why: Fitzgerald's manuscript reads “you write because you've got something to say,” punctuated with a semicolon; the version that circulates today swaps in “you have” and a comma — a small smoothing that has become the standard form. See the notebook transcription ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Fitzgerald really did write this thought down — it's entry 330 of his own notebooks, under “Epigrams, Wisecracks, and Jokes” — the only fabrication is the tidied-up punctuation. See Wikiquote's citation ↗ to the same entry.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Fitzgerald was a compulsive list-keeper. Alongside his novels and stories, he filled notebooks with overheard remarks, jokes, character sketches, and one-line observations, sorted into categories he labeled A through Q — things like “Feelings and Emotions,” “Descriptions of Girls,” and “Epigrams, Wisecracks, and Jokes,” the section this line comes from.

None of this material was meant for publication as-is; Fitzgerald mined it for dialogue and description in his fiction. It reached readers only after his death — first in a slim 1945 selection edited by his friend and critic Edmund Wilson, then in full in 1978 — which is why a private, off-the-cuff notebook entry can now be quoted, in slightly tidied form, as one of his best-known lines about writing.
